blocks.text: Biologists group living things so that evolutionary relationships are easier to see. In 1969 Robert Whittaker placed organisms in five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. Monera held the prokaryotes, cells without a nucleus. The other four kingdoms held eukaryotes. The printed textbook spells the author's first name Rebert; the person named is Robert Whittaker.

In 1990 Carl Woese argued that prokaryotes are not one group. He separated them into Archaea and Bacteria and arranged all life into three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya. Archaea and Bacteria are both prokaryotic, but they differ in membrane chemistry, cell walls and genetics. The textbook states that Archaea and Bacteria evolved separately from a common ancestor, and that molecular evidence places archaea closer to eukaryotes than to bacteria. It then says Eukarya evolved from Archaea after archaea had split from Bacteria. The evolutionary tree in the same section can also be read as Archaea and Eukarya as sister branches after that split. Both readings are recorded; neither is silently replaced.

blocks.title: Phylogeny
blocks.text: Phylogeny is the evolutionary relationship among organisms. A diagram of that relationship is a phylogenetic tree, also called an evolutionary tree.
Domain Archaea

In the five-kingdom system these organisms sat inside Monera. The name comes from Greek archaios, ancient. They are prokaryotes that diverged from bacteria very early. Cells range from about 0.1 micrometres to more than 15 micrometres across. Some form filaments or clusters up to about 200 micrometres long. Shapes include spheres, rods, spirals, lobed cells and rectangles. Reproduction is asexual: binary fission, multiple fission, fragmentation or budding. Mitosis and meiosis do not occur. They were once called archaebacteria.
What makes an archaeal cell different

The cell membrane uses ether links between glycerol and branched hydrocarbon chains. Those membranes stay stable in harsh conditions. Bacteria and Eukarya use ester links and unbranched chains. Archaeal walls lack cellulose and peptidoglycan. They use other polysaccharides and proteins, and some have pseudopeptidoglycan. Bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan, a polymer of sugars and amino acids. When a eukaryotic wall is present it is cellulose in plants or chitin in fungi.

rows: The membrane used by bacteria and eukaryotes

blocks.text: Archaea share some genetic sequences and control features with eukaryotes, which is why they are placed nearer Eukarya than Bacteria. Their distinctive metabolism includes methanogenesis, the production of methane. That process is not found in bacteria or eukaryotes. Bacteria instead show photosynthesis, nitrogen fixation and fermentation. Eukaryotic metabolism is usually more elaborate and includes cellular respiration, photosynthesis in plants and algae, and fermentation.
Major groups

items: Methanogens produce methane as a metabolic by-product.
Halobacteria live in extremely salty environments.
Thermococci live in hot environments.
The text names Thaumarchaeota and their role in the nitrogen cycle.

blocks.title: A label that does not match the text
blocks.text: The figure of major archaeal groups is labelled Methanogens, Halobacteria, Thermoplasmata and Thermococci. The paragraph names Thaumarchaeota rather than Thermoplasmata. The lesson keeps both wordings and does not treat them as the same group.

blocks.title: Why archaea matter
blocks.text: Species that tolerate strong acid or alkali are sources of enzymes that still work in harsh conditions. DNA-replication enzymes from such cells copy DNA quickly at high temperature in the laboratory. Methanogens digest sewage without oxygen and produce biogas. Acid-loving archaea are used to release gold, cobalt and copper from ores. Much of the gas in the human intestine comes from methanogen metabolism.
Domain Bacteria

In the five-kingdom system these organisms were also placed in Monera. They are the true bacteria. They are prokaryotic: no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. The wall is peptidoglycan, which holds the cell's shape. The chromosome is a single circular DNA molecule in the nucleoid. Many cells also carry plasmids, small circular DNA molecules that can move from one bacterium to another and add genetic variety.

Division is usually binary fission, one cell becoming two. Nutrition is autotrophic, including photosynthesis, or heterotrophic, including decay of organic matter. Cells occur alone, in pairs (diplococci), in chains (streptococci), in clusters (staphylococci) or in other species-specific arrangements. Many swim with one or more flagella. Pili and fimbriae are hair-like structures used to attach to surfaces or to pass genetic material.

items: Oxygen use: obligate aerobes, obligate anaerobes, facultative anaerobes, microaerophiles or aerotolerant anaerobes. Some ferment when oxygen is absent.
Some tolerate extremes of heat (thermophiles), salt (halophiles) or acidity (acidophiles).
Some cause disease in humans, animals or plants by toxins or other virulence factors.
Others live with a partner: mutualism, where both benefit, or commensalism, where one benefits and the other is not harmed.

blocks.text: Four forms

blocks.alt: Four original outlines: a sphere (coccus), a rod (bacillus), a comma (vibrio) and a spiral (spirillum).
blocks.caption: Original diagram of the four bacterial forms named in this topic.
blocks.long_description: Cocci are spherical. Bacilli are rod-shaped. Vibrios are comma-shaped. Spirilla are spiral-shaped. These outlines are drawn for this lesson. They are not photographs from the textbook.

blocks.text: Major groups, with examples from the text

items: Proteobacteria, for example Escherichia coli, Rhizobium and Helicobacter pylori.
Firmicutes, for example Bacillus subtilis, Lactobacillus and Clostridium botulinum.
Actinobacteria, for example Streptomyces and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Cyanobacteria, for example Anabaena and Spirulina.
Spirochaetes, for example Treponema pallidum.
Acidobacteria, for example Acidobacterium.
Aquificae, for example Aquifex pyrophilus.

blocks.text: Domain Eukarya

Eukarya contains organisms whose cells have a nucleus bounded by a membrane, plus organelles that have their own membranes. Those organelles include mitochondria and, in plants and algae, chloroplasts. The endoplasmic reticulum, the Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and peroxisomes are also present. A cytoskeleton of microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments supports the cell, lets it move and moves materials inside it.

The DNA is in several linear chromosomes and is packaged with histone proteins. Most eukaryotes reproduce sexually by meiosis and fertilisation, which mixes genes. Some also reproduce asexually by mitosis, giving genetically identical offspring. In multicellular eukaryotes, cells specialise into tissues and organs. The textbook's numbered list of these features skips item 4 and goes from 3 to 5. The lesson does not invent a missing fourth point.

blocks.title: Endosymbiosis
blocks.text: The textbook says eukaryotes arose by endosymbiosis: a host cell took in prokaryotic cells that became mitochondria and chloroplasts and stayed as partners.

rows: Eukaryotic, with a nucleus and organelles

blocks.text: Recap

items: Whittaker's 1969 scheme used five kingdoms and put all prokaryotes in Monera.
Woese's 1990 scheme uses three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
Archaea differ from bacteria in membrane ether links, the absence of peptidoglycan, and methanogenesis.
Bacteria are described by wall, chromosome, plasmids, fission, shape, arrangement, flagella, pili, respiration, extremes, disease and symbiosis.
Eukarya have nuclei, organelles, linear chromosomes with histones, and usually sexual reproduction.

blocks.prompt: Without looking back, name the three domains and one feature that separates Archaea from Bacteria.
blocks.explanation: A complete answer names Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya, and one real difference such as ether versus ester membrane links, peptidoglycan, or methanogenesis.
